A recurring class of bug here: a library quietly fetches its runtime assets from
a public CDN. It makes the feature require connectivity, ships bytes we cannot
version or audit, and — in the worst cases — tells a third party what the user
is doing. Six instances were found and fixed in `cdn-egress-fixes-2026-08-02`;
the detector work is `egress-monitor-origin-axis-2026-08-02`.

This page is how to audit for it without reaching a confident wrong answer,
which is easy to do here in **both** directions.

## The URL is not in our code — scan the BUILT dist

The instinct is to grep the source. That structurally cannot work, and knowing
why tells you where to look instead.

Every one of these URLs is a **default baked into a dependency**:

| library | the default it carries |
| --- | --- |
| `@monaco-editor/loader` | `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/monaco-editor@0.55.1/min/vs` |
| `vditor` | `https://unpkg.com/vditor@<ver>` |
| `@excalidraw/excalidraw` | `ASSETS_FALLBACK_URL` on `esm.sh` |
| `emoji-mart` | `https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@emoji-mart/data@latest/...` |

Our code's only involvement is *failing to override* it. So the string appears
in our repo for the first time in the built bundle. That is why
`lint:no-cdn-egress` (`scripts/check-no-cdn-egress.mjs`) scans
`apps/operator-vite`'s built dist rather than the tree.

The per-library source guards (`vditor-cdn.test.ts`, `monaco-cdn.test.ts`,
`porcupine-cdn.test.ts`) are still correct and still worth having — but note
what they actually assert: *"every entry point passes an explicit `cdn`"*. They
work only because someone had **already identified** the library and the option.
They cannot discover the next one.

## A bundle hit is a DISCOVERY, never a verdict

This is the single most important thing on this page, and the easiest mistake to
make with a scanner in hand.

`cdn-egress-fixes-2026-08-02` D-004 settled it: **only a runtime resource-timing
read can decide this class.** Every fix works by overriding a URL at runtime — an
AMD loader path, `options.cdn`, `EXCALIDRAW_ASSET_PATH`, a `math.engine` pin.
The library's default string is therefore *still in the bundle after the fix
lands*. Presence proves nothing, and absence proves nothing.

Concretely: of the six audited findings, **two were false positives** —
`emoji-mart` and `speech-rule-engine`. Both were proven **not live** at runtime,
and both of their URLs are in the bundle as you read this. Acting on the grep
would have meant two pointless mirroring changes.

The pattern in both was identical: a real CDN URL sits in the bundle, but the
code path that would fetch it is never taken — because the import is a bare
specifier Vite resolves at build time (emoji-mart), or because the URL lives in
a bundle gated behind a config we do not select (speech-rule-engine is in
vditor's MathJax bundle; we pin `math.engine: 'katex'`).

So the workflow is:

1. the scan says **"here is a candidate nobody has classified"**;
2. you **establish liveness at runtime**;
3. then you either fix it, or baseline it with the runtime verdict written down.

`scripts/no-cdn-egress-baseline.json` encodes exactly that: every row carries a
`reason` and a `status` of `inert` | `not-live-verified` | `unresolved`, so a
later reader can tell a row that was *checked and cleared* from one that has
simply *never been looked at*. A bare allowlist would erase that distinction.

## Establishing liveness: the probe-plan technique

Static evidence cannot distinguish "fix works" from "fix broken" for any item in
this class, so verification has to drive the real surface. What worked, twice:

1. Create a throwaway plan whose **content triggers the suspect code path** — a
   ```` ```plantuml ```` block, four `$$…$$` math expressions, a markmap block.
2. Render it through the **real production surface** (`/admin/plans`) in a
   headless Tauri instance (`scripts/verify-tauri-headless.sh`, driven with
   `tauri-agent-tools`).
3. Call `performance.clearResourceTimings()` **first**.
4. Assert the **causal chain**, not mere absence: the content demonstrably
   rendered (a sentinel string, `katexNodes === 4`) **AND** the egress absent.
5. Archive the probe plan (`plans:set-archived`) afterwards.

Step 4 is the one people skip. **Absence of a request proves nothing if the
surface never rendered** — a broken probe and a clean result look identical.

Note `plans:new`'s dedup will block a second probe plan sharing tokens like
"egress/probe/scratch"; `force: true` is correct there, with the reason recorded.

## Two traps that make a scanner silently pass

Both produce a clean-looking result on a dirty tree, which is the worst possible
failure for a detector.

### 1. grep skips minified chunks as binary

GNU grep classifies the minified chunks in `dist/assets/` as **binary** and skips
them, printing nothing at all — not even a zero count — for strings that ARE
present. A grep-based guard would pass vacuously forever and look exactly like a
clean run. This has been independently recorded on this box more than once.

`grep -a` is the shell workaround. The guard instead reads the bytes in Node,
which removes the failure mode rather than tiptoeing around it — and it
**refuses a zero-finding scan** as a `SENSOR FAILURE`, because a real dist always
carries at least the vendored mirrors' own CDN constants. A dead sensor and a
clean run must never be indistinguishable.

### 2. "any non-local origin" drowns you in inert hits

The runtime monitor's rule (`classifyEgress`'s `foreignOrigin` axis) is *any
origin not in the local allowlist is a finding, regardless of path*. That is
right for a **runtime** entry, where something actually fetched.

Applied to a **static** scan it yields **~500 hits on a correct tree**: 267
`www.w3.org` SVG namespace declarations, 60 `github.com` links in vendored
comments, doc links to `mermaid.js.org` and `react.dev`, JSON-Schema `$id`s. All
inert. A guard that reports 500 findings on day one is a guard someone silences.

The discriminator is that the URL's **path must look fetchable** — an asset
extension, or a versioned package path like `/pkg@1.2.3/` (which catches
extensionless CDN bases such as `.../monaco-editor@0.55.1/min/vs`). That cuts
~500 to 24 with no loss of signal: every one of the six known findings is
asset-shaped, and none of the inert mentions are.

Two shapes worth recognising by eye, because both look alarming and are not:

- **`https://github.com/owner/repo/blob/master/thing.js`** — a `/blob/` URL is an
  HTML *page*, not a raw asset. In practice it is a source-attribution comment.
- **`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ajv-validator/ajv/.../data.json#`** — a
  JSON-Schema `$id`, used as a registry key and never dereferenced. The trailing
  `#` (empty JSON-pointer fragment) is the giveaway.

## The three legs are complementary, not alternatives

Each covers a blind spot the others structurally cannot. Shipping one and
calling it done leaves a hole:

| leg | catches | blind to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **static bundle scan** (`lint:no-cdn-egress`) | code **nobody ran** | whether the URL is actually fetched |
| **runtime egress monitor** (`egress-monitor.ts`) | dynamically-built URLs; proves **liveness** | any path no test exercised |
| **CSP** (`tauri.conf.json`) | **prevents** rather than observes | only the packaged shell |

The static leg exists because Monaco fetched 0.55.1 from jsdelivr for months and
**no monitor ever saw it** — nobody opened the Gym while a monitor was installed.

Conversely the runtime leg exists because the static one cannot decide liveness,
which is the whole first half of this page.

## The egress monitor has two orthogonal axes

`libs/generic/desktop-ipc/src/egress-monitor.ts` audits two different invariants.
Keep them separate; collapsing them into one number destroys the triage signal.

- **`ipcEscape`** (transport) — *an `/api/*` call must travel over IPC, never
  HTTP.* Correctly suppressed unless `expectsIpc`, since HTTP is sanctioned in a
  browser shell.
- **`foreignOrigin`** (destination) — *no request may go to a host we do not
  own.* A bug in **every** shell, so it does **not** inherit that suppression.

For years the monitor was blind to the vditor class by construction, in two
lines: a same-origin filter discarded the CDN request in the dev shell, and an
`/api/` path filter discarded it in the packaged shell. It filtered out the
entire class as its first act — precisely because those requests are someone
else's API. `foreignOrigin` runs **before** that narrowing.

Both axes keep a **three-valued verdict** (`clean` / `breach` / `unknown`), where
`unknown` is a failure gated behind a proof-of-life control request. Same
principle as the scanner's `SENSOR FAILURE`: a zero from an unproven sensor is
not a pass.

## Fixing one, once liveness is established

The established shape (`cdn-egress-fixes-2026-08-02` D-001/D-002):

1. **Mirror the whole vendor dist** into the app's `public/` via the postinstall
   /prebuild mirror script — not the subset one screen happens to request. These
   libraries lazily pull more assets the moment content demands them.
2. **Point the library's configurable base at the local mirror** at *every* entry
   point, and add a guard test asserting that, in the `vditor-cdn.test.ts` shape.
3. **Pin third-party downloads by immutable ref + checksum.** Porcupine's `v3.0`
   tag serves a *different* model of *exactly the same byte length* as `v4.0` —
   size is not an identity check, only the checksum is.

Two failure modes to expect:

- **A fallback that is appended unconditionally.** Excalidraw's
  `ASSETS_FALLBACK_URL` stays in the candidate list even once
  `EXCALIDRAW_ASSET_PATH` is set, so an *incomplete* mirror does not 404 loudly —
  it silently falls through to `esm.sh` and the app looks fixed while still
  fetching. Mirror completely, and verify at runtime.
- **Mirroring a package does not fix URLs baked into files inside it.** vditor's
  markmap loader still resolves `d3` from jsdelivr from inside our local mirror.

When the egress is **content** rather than latency — PlantUML posted document
text to `plantuml.com`, Excalidraw embeds tell Twitter what you are viewing — the
correct default is **fail closed** (D-003).

## Running it

```bash
npm run lint:no-cdn-egress          # builds operator-vite, then scans (~60s)
npm run lint:no-cdn-egress -- --dist DIR   # scan an existing dist (fast)
npm run lint:no-cdn-egress:report   # list every finding, exit 0
npm run lint:no-cdn-egress:update   # re-generate the baseline
```

The baseline is a **ratchet, not an amnesty**: rows are expected to be removed as
fixes land, and the guard reports removals so the floor drops behind you. It
never auto-accepts an addition. `--update` carries hand-written classification
(`status`, `reason`) forward rather than resetting it.

It runs in GitHub Actions (`test.yml`), next to `lint:bundle-budget`. The
green-checkpoint runs only a named lint set and includes neither — that is the
convention for bundle-level guards, not an oversight.

## If you add a guard like this, negative-control it

Prove it **fails** on a mutated copy before trusting it, and do that **out of
tree** (a synthetic fixture dir, or `cp -al` of a dist plus one added file) —
never by temporarily breaking a real file, because git-sync sweeps the whole tree
and would commit the broken intermediate.

`packages/operator-core/lib/no-cdn-egress-guard.test.ts` does this. It also pins
the content-hash normalization, which was gotten wrong twice in opposite
directions while writing it — too loose (`{8,}`) ate the real filename word
`third-languages.js`; too strict (digit **and** uppercase) missed the genuine
hash `CmCJkiVB`, which would report an unchanged bundle as a new finding and fail
the gate spuriously. The second is the worse direction: a guard that cries wolf
is a guard that gets muted.
